case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the government may treat a returning lawful permanent resident as an applicant for admission under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) based on proof that the person committed a § 1182(a)(2) offense—even if the government lacks conviction-level proof at the time of the border encounter and instead relies on later-developed evidence.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C) (exceptions under which an LPR is treated as seeking admission), especially § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) (LPR has 'committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2)'); and 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2) (criminal grounds of inadmissibility, including crimes involving moral turpitude).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Attorney General argues that Congress adopted a conduct-based admission framework in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v): a returning LPR can be treated as seeking admission if he has 'committed' a § 1182(a)(2) offense, which does not require the government to possess or present conviction-level proof at the border. The government maintains that immigration authorities may defer inspection/parole the person and then, in subsequent removal proceedings, prove that the LPR committed the qualifying offense (including using evidence that becomes available after entry), consistent with border-security and administrability needs.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Lau argues that an LPR should not be stripped of returning-resident protections and reclassified as seeking admission unless the government can prove the § 1101(a)(13)(C) exception under the correct (and, in his view, clear-and-convincing) standard using properly limited evidence; he also contends the government failed to preserve any challenge to the applicable burden of proof because it assumed below that clear-and-convincing evidence applies. Separately, he maintains that the dispositive issue is whether his offense actually qualifies as a crime involving moral turpitude under § 1182(a)(2), making the presented question a poor vehicle because the case outcome ultimately turns on that classification regardless of the timing/burden framework.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan are right that the phrase “has committed” is conduct-based and, standing alone, does not impose a conviction or contemporaneous-proof requirement. But that does not resolve the structural question Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press: § 1101(a)(13)(C) is framed as a narrow, inspection-tethered departure from the default rule that returning LPRs are not treated as seeking admission, and reading (C)(v) to allow DHS to invoke the exception first and prove it later risks collapsing that default into a conditional presumption. Vartelas, as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, counsels caution about attaching severe travel-triggered consequences absent a clear congressional statement, and I do not see Congress clearly authorizing a parole-and-prove-later regime that retroactively flips the LPR’s procedural posture based on later-developed evidence. The Government’s administrability and public-safety concerns (Justice Alito) are real, but the INA already supplies an enforcement path through § 1227 when DHS cannot establish at the point of return that it may lawfully treat the LPR as an applicant for admission.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s best point is structural: as he argues, § 1101(a)(13)(C) operates at inspection and is meant to be a narrow, administrable departure from the returning-LPR default. But that institutional intuition cannot justify adding a timing or “proof-in-hand” requirement Congress did not write into (C)(v), which asks whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense—language that, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, contrasts with provisions where Congress expressly uses “convicted” or other administrable triggers. Vartelas, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, confirms IIRIRA replaced Fleuti’s atextual framework with the statute’s enumerated exceptions; it does not authorize us to graft onto (v) a clear-statement rule about when DHS must have evidence. The availability of § 1227 removability, highlighted by the Chief, is a policy alternative, not a textual limitation on Congress’s choice to attach inadmissibility-based consequences when the predicate fact—commission of the offense—ultimately is proven.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point—that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is an inspection-tethered determination with enumerated carveouts—is the strongest case for Respondent, but it cannot supply a timing requirement Congress did not write. Subsection (C)(v) asks whether the LPR “has committed” a § 1182(a)(2) offense; as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, that conduct-based, perfect-tense phrasing contrasts with provisions that hinge on a “conviction,” and it reads naturally as a predicate that can be established in ensuing proceedings rather than at primary inspection. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance/fairness concerns and her invocation of Vartelas underscore the stakes, but Vartelas principally confirms that IIRIRA displaced Fleuti with the six statutory exceptions, and it does not justify adding an atextual “provable-at-the-border” limitation that would blunt Congress’s evident aim of meaningful border scrutiny. So long as DHS bears the ultimate burden in removal proceedings to prove the (C)(v) predicate before imposing consequences, I see no textual or precedential basis to freeze the inquiry at the port of entry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett make the strongest point for Petitioner that “has committed” is conduct-based and not, on its face, conviction- or inspection-proof-based; I take that seriously. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 1101(a)(13)(C) is framed as a protective default for returning LPRs with narrow, inspection-tethered carveouts, and allowing DHS to treat an LPR as seeking admission first and substantiate (C)(v) later functionally converts that default into a conditional presumption—an error-prone regime with grave liberty and reliance costs. Vartelas reinforces the severity and reliance-disrupting nature of travel-triggered consequences for LPRs, so absent a clearer congressional signal I will not read (C)(v) to authorize “parole-and-prove-later” despite the textual plausibility Petitioner identifies. Justice Alito’s public-safety/workability concerns are real, but they do not justify diluting Congress’s returning-resident protection when § 1227 provides an established pathway if the Government cannot lawfully apply the admission framework at the border.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s structural concern—that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is an inspection-tethered classification and should not become a “parole-and-prove-later” regime—is the strongest point for Respondent, but I still do not see a textual hook for a contemporaneous-proof requirement. As Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Congress knows how to require conviction- or border-time administrability triggers; instead it chose conduct-focused, perfect-tense language (“has committed”) in (C)(v), which reads as a predicate that can be determined in ensuing proceedings with the Government bearing the burden. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance/Vartelas argument reinforces caution about expanding travel consequences, but Vartelas largely confirms that IIRIRA displaced Fleuti with the enumerated exceptions rather than adding a timing limitation that Congress did not write. The workability and burden-allocation concerns Roberts and Justice Jackson raise are real, yet they are better addressed through the INA’s procedural protections and proof burdens in removal proceedings than by judicially inserting timing words into (v).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts offers the strongest counterargument: that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is an inspection-tethered classification and that allowing DHS to invoke (C)(v) without proof in hand risks a “parole-and-prove-later” regime that erodes the protective default. But under a textualist/originalist approach, that structural concern cannot supply an atextual timing limitation where Congress chose the conduct-based phrase “has committed,” rather than the conviction- or admission-triggering language it uses elsewhere, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize. Vartelas, as Justice Sotomayor notes, underscores the seriousness of travel consequences, yet it chiefly confirms that IIRIRA replaced Fleuti with the enumerated exceptions; it does not create a clear-statement rule rewriting (C)(v) into “provable at primary inspection.” The availability of § 1227, highlighted by the Chief, is a policy alternative but not a textual constraint, and any administrability concerns are better handled by insisting the Government carry its burden in removal proceedings rather than by adding words to the statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s structural concern—that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is an inspection-tethered classification and that our reading could invite a “parole-and-prove-later” regime—is the strongest point for Respondent, but I still do not find a statutory hook for importing a contemporaneous-proof requirement into (C)(v). As Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress chose the conduct-based perfect-tense phrase “has committed,” and where Congress wanted administrable border-time triggers it typically used conviction-based language; I am reluctant, as an institutional matter, to add a timing condition Congress did not enact. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance/fairness concerns are serious, and Vartelas underscores the stakes, but Vartelas primarily confirms that IIRIRA displaced Fleuti with enumerated exceptions rather than creating a clear-statement rule that the Government must possess proof at primary inspection. The better legitimacy-protecting constraint is to insist DHS ultimately carry its burden in the removal proceeding (and to rely on existing procedural limits on parole/detention), not to rewrite (C)(v) into “provable at the border.”

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s structural concern—that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is an inspection-tethered classification and that allowing later proof risks a “parole-and-prove-later” regime—is the strongest argument for Respondent, but it still cannot supply the missing textual hook for a contemporaneous-proof requirement. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Congress wrote (C)(v) in perfect-tense, conduct-focused terms (“has committed”), and where Congress wanted administrable, point-in-time triggers it used conviction-based language; importing a border-moment evidentiary prerequisite would add words the statute does not contain. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance/fairness and Vartelas-based caution underscore the need for careful procedure and for the Government to carry its burden in removal proceedings, but Vartelas confirms that IIRIRA replaced Fleuti with the enumerated exceptions rather than creating an atextual clear-statement rule limiting (C)(v) to what DHS can prove at primary inspection. The availability of § 1227, highlighted by the Chief, is a policy alternative, not a statutory constraint on the meaning of (C)(v).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right that “has committed” is conduct-based and, standing alone, does not require a conviction or explicitly fix proof to the moment of primary inspection. But as the Chief Justice stresses, § 1101(a)(13)(C) is a protective default for returning LPRs, and the statutory question is when the Government may “regard” the person as seeking admission—a classification that, in real operation, is made at the border and should not be converted into a parole-and-prove-later regime absent clearer congressional authorization. Justice Thomas’s point that we should not “add words” overlooks that the timing constraint here comes from the function and structure of the “regarded as seeking an admission” determination, not from judicially rewriting (C)(v). Vartelas, as Justice Sotomayor notes, reinforces my reluctance to read IIRIRA to impose severe, travel-triggered procedural consequences based on later-developed proof when Congress left intact an alternative enforcement path through § 1227 removability.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) sets out narrow, enumerated exceptions to the general rule that a returning LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission,” and the structure and verb tenses of those exceptions indicate the government must determine at the time of entry whether an exception applies, rather than retroactively converting an admitted LPR into an applicant for admission based on later-developed evidence. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v)’s “has committed” to authorize post-entry, later-proven conduct determinations would broaden an exception Congress used to cabin Fleuti’s former “entry” doctrine and would risk undermining settled reliance interests and institutional regularity in LPR travel, contrary to the narrowing impulse reflected in § 1101(a)(13)(C). The government remains free to proceed under § 1227 (deportability) if it cannot make the requisite showing at the border, preserving both administrability and federalism-sensitive limits without stretching § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v). This narrower construction adheres to Congress’s codification/abrogation framework and avoids a sweeping rule that would destabilize returning-resident protections.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” which is conduct-based and does not require the government to possess conviction-level proof at the moment of the border encounter. Congress enacted IIRIRA in 1996 to narrow the judge-made protections of Rosenberg v. Fleuti and to restore meaningful border scrutiny of returning LPRs with qualifying criminal conduct; reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) to demand contemporaneous conviction-proof would add atextual limits and frustrate that design. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) or § 1182(a)(2) imposes a timing rule barring the government from proving “committed” in later removal proceedings with later-developed evidence, so long as it ultimately satisfies the applicable burden of proof. The respondent’s vehicle and burden-of-proof objections do not change the statute’s original public meaning: “committed” denotes the underlying offense conduct, not the government’s evidentiary posture at inspection.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” and that phrasing is conduct-based rather than limited to what the government can prove at the precise moment of the border encounter. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) or § 1182(a)(2) imposes a timing rule requiring conviction-level proof at inspection; the government may parole/defer inspection and then, in later removal proceedings, prove the qualifying conduct, which aligns with IIRIRA’s purpose of restoring meaningful border scrutiny after Fleuti’s judge-made insulation of brief trips. Allowing later-developed evidence avoids the practical and public-safety vulnerability of forcing admission when reliable proof exists but cannot be marshaled instantly at the port of entry. Congress’s 1996 codification/abrogation of the Fleuti doctrine in § 1101(a)(13)(C) supports interpreting “has committed” to authorize this admission framework without a border-only evidentiary constraint.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) creates narrow, enumerated exceptions to the general rule that returning lawful permanent residents are not treated as applicants for admission, and the Government bears the burden to establish an exception before stripping an LPR of that protected status. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) (“has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2)”) to allow admission-status to hinge on later-developed evidence—rather than what the Government can properly establish at the time it invokes the exception—invites arbitrary deprivations of settled residence and undermines the fairness and reliance interests Congress preserved when it only partially displaced Fleuti in IIRIRA. Vartelas confirms that IIRIRA changed the framework but also cautions against interpretations that attach severe immigration consequences to travel in a manner that disrupts settled expectations without clear congressional command. Given the grave practical consequences for LPRs and the risk of error, the Government should not be permitted to treat an LPR as seeking admission under § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) absent proof satisfying the governing standard at the time it triggers that classification.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” and that conduct-based phrasing does not, on its face, impose a border-encounter timing requirement or a conviction-at-the-port limitation. Congress enacted § 1101(a)(13)(C) in IIRIRA to narrow Fleuti’s insulation of returning LPRs from meaningful border scrutiny, and reading (v) to allow DHS to treat the person as seeking admission once the government later proves the qualifying conduct in removal proceedings better fits that design and is more workable administratively. The statutory question is thus about the government’s ability to establish the exception in proceedings (with whatever burden of proof applies), not about what quantum of proof must be in hand at the moment of inspection, and nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) requires the latter. This approach also preserves statutory coherence with § 1182(a)(2), which often uses conviction-focused triggers but is incorporated here through Congress’s distinct choice of the broader term “committed.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) asks whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” and “committed” is conduct-based language that does not, on its face, demand conviction-level proof at the border encounter. Congress enacted § 1101(a)(13)(C) in IIRIRA to narrow Fleuti’s judge-made returning-resident insulation and restore meaningful border scrutiny for LPRs with criminal conduct, so it would be odd to freeze the government’s authority at the moment of inspection rather than allow the exception to be established in subsequent proceedings. Nothing in § 1101(a)(13)(C) supplies a timing limitation on the evidence the government may use to prove the exception, and absent clear congressional direction courts should not add one—especially in a way that would expand judicially crafted protections Congress chose to curtail. While due process and burden-of-proof questions may remain for the agency and courts below, the statutory question presented is best answered by adhering to the provision’s plain meaning and IIRIRA’s evident design.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) adopts a conduct-based trigger—an LPR is treated as seeking admission if he “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2)”—and the text does not require the government to possess conviction-level proof at the moment of the border encounter. After IIRIRA, Congress displaced Fleuti’s broad protection and instead specified six exceptions, reflecting a practical and administrable regime in which inspection/parole at the border may be followed by removal proceedings where the government proves the exception based on the evidentiary record developed there. Vartelas confirms that the post-1996 framework turns on the statutory exceptions in § 1101(a)(13)(C), not a judge-made “innocent, casual, and brief” doctrine, and nothing in that decision suggests the timing of proof is fixed at the border encounter. Requiring conviction-level proof at the border would be atextual and would undermine Congress’s evident purpose to restore meaningful border scrutiny for criminal conduct, while still leaving the ultimate factual determination to the adjudicatory process in later proceedings.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed an offense identified in section 1182(a)(2),” and “committed” is conduct-based language, not a conviction-based requirement; Congress elsewhere in § 1182(a)(2) knows how to require a “conviction” when it wants to. Reading § 1101(a)(13)(C) against IIRIRA’s partial abrogation/codification of Fleuti confirms Congress’s aim to restore meaningful border scrutiny for LPRs with disqualifying criminal conduct, rather than making the applicability of (C)(v) depend on what proof happens to exist at the moment of inspection. Vartelas v. Holder reinforces that § 1101(a)(13)(C) is the governing post-1996 framework for when an LPR is treated as seeking admission, displacing broader Fleuti-era protections.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1101(a)(13)(C) establishes that an LPR “shall not be regarded as seeking an admission” unless the Government proves one of the enumerated exceptions, and treating an LPR as an applicant based on later-developed evidence risks eroding that returning-resident protection through a parole-and-prove-later regime inconsistent with procedural fairness. Attorney General) without relying on the happenstance of evidence obtained only after the encounter to justify treating the person as seeking admission in the first place. This approach preserves Congress’s post-IIRIRA framework while ensuring practical, administrable safeguards against arbitrary deprivation of LPR protections, consistent with the fairness concerns that animated Fleuti and remain relevant after its partial codification/abrogation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(5) provides that a returning LPR “shall not” be regarded as seeking admission unless he “has committed an offense identified in” 8 U.S.C. § 1182(a)(2); Congress’s choice of “committed,” rather than “convicted,” indicates a conduct-based trigger, not a conviction-only rule. Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the returning LPR “has committed” an offense identified in § 1182(a)(2), not whether the government had conviction-level proof or complete evidence at the instant of inspection; Congress’s choice of “committed” is naturally read as conduct-based and would be undermined by a rule freezing the record at the border.
